extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy fans, and general pop-culture readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what makes stand-up comedy (and comedians) successful, ethical, and culturally resonant, as argued in a pop-culture opinion piece. Focuses on approaches to targets, tone, audience relation, and adapting to changing norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny independent of 'saying whatever you want'
rubrics_metrics.description: People weren’t all that funny when they could say whatever they wanted to say; blaming 'cancel culture' often signals you simply weren't funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a comedian claims cancel culture ruined their career, the implication (per Katt Williams) is that their material was not strong enough to survive scrutiny; humor should stand on its own merits rather than rely on unfiltered license. The article opens and returns to the line: “there’s no cancel culture” and “people weren’t all that funny when they could say whatever they wanted to say.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't exploit or trivialize marginalized people
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid exploiting — and, by doing so, trivializing — the feelings of marginalized people for laughs from the general audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using marginalized people's pain as a cheap punchline is presented as a harmful anti-pattern; it invites rightful criticism (e.g., Dave Chappelle's transphobic jokes were criticized). Good comedy refrains from deriving laughs by belittling those without power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedy to confront problems — comedy + commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can be a vehicle for social change; comics can confront problems head-on and need not separate comedy from commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Katt Williams is credited for using his microphone to address issues directly rather than simply exploiting targets. The piece argues that 'comedy and commentary need not be mutually exclusive' and that effective comedy can combine insight and critique with humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place yourself on the same level as the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics on the stage should place themselves on the same level as their audience rather than elevating themselves above them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being on the same level fosters connection and prevents punching down; Williams emphasizes that effective comics don't act as though their feelings are inherently more important than the audience's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reveling in misery or self-importance as the main comic strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedies that primarily revel in misery or invite viewers to 'relish in their own misery' are not good and can alienate audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article critiques work (e.g., Ricky Gervais' After Life) that centers the comedian's suffering in a way that encourages viewers’ self-indulgent misery rather than genuine humor or insight. Such approaches make audiences feel the comedian is solipsistic rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace inward-looking, self-deprecating authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Younger performers succeeding in current climate often use self-deprecation and inward-looking material (e.g., John Mulaney, Bo Burnham).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece highlights that comics who mine their own experiences and flaws (self-deprecation, irony about privilege, examining self-centeredness) are resonating with modern audiences and are part of comedy’s future as controversial figures fall away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony and critique of privilege rather than straightforward entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Poking fun at privilege and self-centeredness (as Bo Burnham does) is presented as a successful tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony that exposes the comedian’s own or their peers' privilege and entitlement can be more effective and culturally acceptable than jokes that celebrate or defend problematic attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use 'cancel culture' as a blanket excuse; be specific and accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'cancel culture' is often vague and hypocritical; it should not be employed as a catch-all defense for poor material or behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Williams argues 'cancellation doesn’t have its own culture' and that invoking 'cancel culture' obscures the real dynamics (power, accountability). Comedians should address specific critiques rather than hiding behind the vague concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize power dynamics and who is doing the policing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cancellation often reflected marginalized communities policing their own culture and pushing back against more powerful figures who had previously silenced them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article points out that what’s labeled 'cancellation' was frequently people of color and those without a voice defending themselves against influential figures. Effective comedians should understand these dynamics rather than dismiss critics as irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to changing audience norms to maintain longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: As controversial figures (e.g., Louis C.K.) leave the stage, newer comedians who align with evolving norms take their place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term success in comedy requires evolving material and approaches that reflect contemporary sensibilities; relying on outdated tactics risks obsolescence.
